1  Introduction

Fine-tuning pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) has become the dominant paradigm in contemporary natural language processing [Howard and Ruder, 2018], allowing large pretrained networks to be efficiently adapted to diverse downstream tasks with limited labelled data [Howard and Ruder, 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Lester et al., 2021]. The fine-tuning objective is commonly cast as an unconstrained optimization problem

minx∈ℝd⁡f⁡(x),\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(x), (1)

where xx denotes the model parameters, dd is the dimension of xx (number of trainable parameters) and f⁡(x)f(x) is the loss.

Algorithms that rely on access to gradients remain the prevailing tools for solving the problem (1). Classical first-order optimizers such as Stochastic Gradient Descent [Robbins and Monro, 1951; Amari, 1993] and Adam [Kingma and Ba, 2014] are widely used because they integrate naturally with backpropagation and offer strong empirical performance [Semenov et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2025].

Despite these advances in stability and the practical convenience afforded by backpropagation, its memory footprint poses a growing practical barrier as model sizes increase [Rajbhandari et al., 2020]. Storing activations and optimizer States for gradient computation can dominate the memory budget: reported measurements indicate that gradient computation for models at the tens-of-billions parameter scale may require approximately 1212 times more memory than inference [Zhu et al., 2023b]. This constraint restricts accessible fine-tuning workflows on resource-limited hardware (for example, edge devices and consumer GPUs) and complicates large-scale distributed training [Zhu et al., 2023a; Gao et al., 2024; Liao et al., 2024].

To mitigate memory pressure, a range of strategies has been explored. One family comprises coordinate-wise or block-coordinate schemes which can reduce the number of gradient parameters from dd to 11 [Richtárik and Takáč, 2014]. However, this comes at the cost of an asymptotic slowdown in convergence by a factor of dd [Li et al., 2018] (see Section 3 for details). One of the most prominent representatives of coordinate methods is BAdam [Luo et al., 2024], which reduces memory consumption by performing block-wise adaptive updates. While this lowers the storage requirements for optimizer States, as is typical for coordinate-wise optimization methods, it introduces a trade-off in the form of slower convergence, with the iteration complexity increasing proportionally to the number of blocks and, in the worst case, to the dimension dd.

Motivated by these memory–convergence trade-offs in first-order schemes, Zero-order (ZO) methods offer a principled alternative. Rather than computing exact gradients via backpropagation, ZO approaches reconstruct directional derivatives (or gradient projections) from function evaluations by perturbing the objective along randomized directions. As a consequence, ZO methods require substantially less memory than coordinate-wise first-order methods such as BAdam [Malladi et al., 2023], since they avoid storing intermediate activations and optimizer States associated with gradient computation. By estimating descent directions using only such finite-difference information, ZO methods eliminate the need for backward passes and the associated storage of intermediate activations. This black-box viewpoint decouples optimization from the internal implementation of the model and enables fine-tuning with substantially smaller memory budgets. Recent work has demonstrated that applying classical ZO updates to LLM fine-tuning can reduce memory consumption by several times compared to standard first-order pipelines [Zhang et al., 2024].

The first recognition of this idea in the context of LLM fine-tuning came with the MeZO [Malladi et al., 2023] method, where the authors employed a ZO SGD [Ghadimi and Lan, 2013] update based on the following gradient estimator:

v⋅⟨∇f​(x),v⟩≈v⋅f⁡(x+τ​v)−f⁡(x−τ​v)2​τ,\displaystyle v\cdot\langle\nabla f(x),v\rangle\approx v\cdot\frac{f(x+\tau v)-f(x-\tau v)}{2\tau}, (2)

where random direction v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d} typically sampled from 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1) [Nesterov and Spokoiny, 2017], and τ>0\tau>0 is the smoothing parameter.

At a high level, ZO-SGD as well as other ZO methods share a similar design philosophy with coordinate approaches, however, rely exclusively on forward-only information to approximate gradients. Estimators of the form (2) constitute a standard design choice for ZO schemes and are widely used in the modern literature [Chen et al., 2017; Malladi et al., 2023; Petrov et al., 2025]. Moreover, in the limit τ→0\tau\rightarrow 0 the method recovers coordinate SGD.

Therefore ZO approaches suffer from inherent limitation: gradient estimates based on random directional derivatives exhibit high variance, similar to coordinate methods. Moreover, as the dimensionality dd increases, the probability that a random direction forms a large angle with the true gradient grows, leading to a further deterioration in the accuracy of the estimated descent direction. In essence, ZO methods obtain information only along a limited set of directions, behaving analogously to coordinate- or block-wise schemes. Consequently, they inherit a principal drawback: the effective convergence rate degrades by a factor of dd [Zhan et al., 2024]. Consequently, until recently, the use of ZO methods were mostly restricted to low-dimensional settings [Wang et al., 2018]. However, in light of modern applications in LLM fine-tuning, where the dimensionality dd reaches 101010^{10} [Seung et al., 2025], this limitation has become even more pronounced.

This work aims to mitigate the restrictive role of variance in ZO schemes. We view the ZO optimization process through the lens of Reinforcement Learning (RL), interpreting the distribution mean of the direction vv as a policy. By introducing a plug-and-play extension to the ZO framework, we enable a memory-efficient exploitation of information from previous iterations to improve the quality of gradient approximation. Our goal is both to provide theoretical insight and to empirically validate the proposed approach in real-world application settings.

Our contributions are as follow:

  • •

    We introduce a novel ZO method, based on optimization of distribution to avoid uninformative directions.

  • •

    We provide theoretical guarantees for the proposed method under the smooth non-convex setup. Novel design leads to non-standard challenges, theoretical analysis and bounds. The resulting convergence guarantees exhibit no dependence on the dimension dd.

  • •

    We empirically evaluate the proposed ZO method on challenging LLM fine-tuning benchmarks, demonstrating their effectiveness and practical relevance.

2  Related Work

2.1 Memory efficient approaches

We note that, beyond ZO approaches, the memory-efficient optimization literature includes several orthogonal techniques, such as gradient quantization to lower precision [Novikov et al., 2023], compression of optimizer statistics [Dettmers et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023], forward gradient learning [Baydin et al., 2022; Silver et al., 2021], greedy layer-wise strategy [Nøkland and Eidnes, 2019], synthetic gradients [Jaderberg et al., 2017] and others [Lv et al., 2024; Boopathy and Fiete, 2022; Hinton, 2022; Singhal et al., 2023].

Nevertheless, ZO methods have emerged as the most effective solutions for memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning [Malladi et al., 2023]. The most apparent distinction among existing ZO approaches lies in the choice of the sampling distribution for the random direction vv. Commonly used options include the uniform distribution over the unit sphere RS(1)∥⋅∥dRS(1)^{d}_{\|\cdot\|} [Flaxman et al., 2004], the standard multivariate Gaussian distribution 𝒩⁡(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0,I) [Ghadimi and Lan, 2013; Nesterov and Spokoiny, 2017], and a uniform discrete distribution over the vectors of the canonical (one-hot) basis [Duchi et al., 2015]. These choices yield unbiased gradient estimators of the smoothed function ff, which form the foundation of the theoretical analyses of the ZO methods.

Recent works have explored complementary strategies for making ZO optimization more practical and memory-efficient. ZO-AdaMM [Chen et al., 2019] generalizes adaptive-moment methods to the gradient-free regime, combining momentum with per-coordinate adaptive step-sizes using only function evaluations. JAGUAR [Veprikov et al., 2024; Petrov et al., 2025] implements a momentum-focused ZO design and related matrix-aware extensions, emphasizing minimal per-iteration oracle cost and memory-efficient updates for large-model fine-tuning.

2.2 ZO optimization with adaptive direction sampling

Recent advances have aimed to inject richer curvature information into ZO procedures to improve stability and convergence. One of the first approaches in this direction was proposed in HiZOO [Zhao et al., 2024]: it augments zero-order gradient (2) with precondition matrix, using a Hessian-informed strategy to mitigate heterogeneous curvature across parameters.

Another recent perspective casts ZO finite-difference procedures as instances of policy optimization. In the work [Qiu et al., 2025], authors show that standard ZO finite-difference estimators are mathematically equivalent to a single-step policy optimization objective and, equivalently, to a REINForCE-style gradient estimator [Williams, 1992] with a particular baseline. Building on this insight, they propose ZoAR method, which incorporates policy-optimization–inspired variance reduction through an averaged baseline and query reuse.

A further contribution is presented in [Seung et al., 2025], which introduces LOREN: a curvature-aware ZO method that formulates gradient preconditioning as adaptive estimation of an anisotropic perturbation distribution, employs a low-rank block-diagonal preconditioner within a natural evolution strategies framework, and uses a REINForCE leave-one-out estimator to improve convergence and search efficiency.

In contrast to these approaches, our method focuses on adaptively learning the mean of the sampling distribution rather than estimating or approximating second-order curvature information. Unlike HiZOO and LOREN, which rely on explicit or implicit Hessian-related preconditioning and therefore introduce additional structural assumptions and memory overhead, our framework remains lightweight and preserves the simplicity of first-order ZO updates. At the same time, compared to policy-optimization–based ZO methods such as ZoAR, which primarily target variance reduction through baselines and query reuse, we directly bias the sampling distribution toward empirically useful directions by learning the distribution mean. This allows us to improve directional alignment without modifying the underlying ZO estimator or increasing algorithmic complexity, making the proposed framework a modular plug-in that can be seamlessly combined with a wide range of existing ZO optimizers.

3  Algorithm and Theoretical Analysis under Directional Setup

3.1 Notation and Assumptions

For any vector x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} we denote by ‖x‖=∑i=1dxi2\|x\|=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_{i}^{2}} the Euclidean l2l_{2} norm. For any non-zero x≠0x\neq 0 we define its normalized version as x¯=x‖x‖\overline{x}=\frac{x}{\|x\|}. We conduct the theoretical analysis in non-convex setting under the standard assumptions [Bertsekas, 1997; Ghadimi and Lan, 2013; Richtárik et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021].

Assumption 1.

Let ff be LL-smooth, i.e., for all x1,x2∈ℝdx_{1},x_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} it holds that: ‖∇f​(x1)−∇f​(x2)‖≤L​‖x1−x2‖.\|\nabla f(x_{1})-\nabla f(x_{2})\|\leq L\|x_{1}-x_{2}\|.

Assumption 2.

Let there exist a minimizer of ff i.e., an x∗x^{*} that f⁡(x)≥f⁡(x∗)f(x)\geq f(x^{*}) holds for all x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

3.2 Motivation

We consider solving the problem (1) using optimization along random directions, i.e., via a Directional Gradient Descent (DGD) [Silver et al., 2021]:

xt+1=xt−γxt⋅vt¯​⟨vt¯,∇f​(xt)⟩,\displaystyle x^{t+1}=x^{t}-\gamma_{x}^{t}\cdot\overline{v^{t}}\langle\overline{v^{t}},\nabla f(x^{t})\rangle, (3)

where the sampling distribution of vtv^{t} is arbitrary. We note that ZO oracle (2) reduces to DGD estimator under the τ→0\tau\to 0 condition. It makes the role of the direction sampling distribution identical in both formulations and allows us to focus on the DGD setup in the theoretical analysis.

Intuitively, the quality of the estimator improves as the sampled direction becomes better aligned with the gradient, and it attains its maximum accuracy in the case of a deterministic choice of vtv^{t} collinear with ∇f​(xt)\nabla f(x^{t}). To formalize this intuition, we introduce the notion of gradient alignment:

Ct:=⟨vt¯,∇f​(xt)¯⟩2,\displaystyle C^{t}:=\left\langle\overline{v^{t}},\overline{\nabla{f(x^{t})}}\right\rangle^{2}, (4)

and use it in Lemma 1, inspired by [Cheng et al., 2021].

Lemma 1.

Under Assumptions 1 and 2 for iterations of DGD (3) the following inequality holds:

∑t=0T−11T​𝔼​[(γxt−L​γxt22)​𝔼​[Ct|ℱt−1]​‖∇f​(xt)‖2]≤f⁡(x0)−f⁡(x∗)T,\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\frac{1}{T}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\gamma_{x}^{t}-\frac{L{\gamma_{x}^{t}}^{2}}{2}\right)\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}\right]\|\nabla f(x^{t})\|^{2}\right]\leq\frac{f(x^{0})-f(x^{*})}{T},

where ℱt\mathcal{F}^{t} is a σ\sigma-algebra generated by {x0,x1,…,xt}\{x^{0},x^{1},\dots,x^{t}\}.

One of its key features is that Lemma 1 applies to an arbitrary sampling distribution. Crucially for our analysis, it does not rely on the unbiasedness of the oracle, in contrast to commonly used approaches [Nesterov and Spokoiny, 2017]. This significantly broadens the range of settings that can be analysed within this framework.

The simplest choice of the sampling distribution is vt∼𝒩⁡(μt≡0,ε2​I)v^{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu^{t}\equiv 0,\varepsilon^{2}I): a Gaussian distribution with zero mean, which yields an unbiased estimator in the DGD setting. After normalizing the sampled vector, this yields a uniform distribution over the unit sphere vt¯∼RS(1)∥⋅∥d\overline{v^{t}}{\sim}RS(1)^{d}_{\|\cdot\|}. Notably, by leveraging Lemma 1, we recover the convergence rate for DGD with vt​∼i.i.d.​𝒩​(0,ε2​I)v^{t}\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,\varepsilon^{2}I) established in [Nesterov and Spokoiny, 2017], as Stated in Corollary 1.

Corollary 1.

Let in the setting of Lemma 1 vt​∼i.i.d.​𝒩​(μt≡0,ε2​I)v^{t}\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(\mu^{t}\equiv 0,\varepsilon^{2}I) and γxt≤12​L\gamma^{t}_{x}\leq\frac{1}{2L}. Then the following bound holds:

𝔼​‖∇f​(x¯T)‖2≤2​dγxt​T​(f⁡(x0)−f⁡(x∗)),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f(\overline{x}^{T})\|^{2}\leq\frac{2d}{\gamma_{x}^{t}T}(f(x^{0})-f(x^{*})),

where x¯T\overline{x}^{T} is chosen uniformly from {x0,x1,…,xt−1}\{x^{0},x^{1},\dots,x^{t-1}\}.

The proof of Corollary 1 is provided in Appendix B and directly reveals that the dd factor arises from 𝔼⁡[Ct|ℱt−1]∼1/d\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}\right]\sim 1/d for vt​∼i.i.d.​𝒩​(0,ε2​I)v^{t}\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,\varepsilon^{2}I).

The above intuition shows that, on the one hand, Lemma 1 indeed captures the variance effect induced by the randomness of the direction, and on the other hand, its application yields tight bounds. This makes expected gradient alignment 𝔼⁡[Ct|ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}\right] a key concept in the analysis of the DGD setup. To obtain theoretical acceleration, it is necessary to maintain this quantity at an 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) level, in contrast to the baseline 𝒪⁡(1/d)\mathcal{O}(1/d) regime. To this end, we propose to leverage information about the objective function obtained during previous iterations by learning the parameters of the sampling distribution and introducing control over them to increase the value of 𝔼⁡[Ct|ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}\right].

Using a Gaussian distribution gives rise to two design choices: adapting the mean vector μt\mu^{t} or the covariance matrix Σt\Sigma^{t}. We focus on learning μt\mu^{t} and fix Σt≡ε2​I\Sigma^{t}\equiv\varepsilon^{2}I, since in the context of memory-efficient optimization storing a full covariance matrix is infeasible, whereas learning the mean vector incurs only an additional 𝒪⁡(d)\mathcal{O}(d) memory overhead, which is acceptable in the ZO setting.

3.3 Theoretical Algorithm

The above mentioned intuition, along with Lemma 1, motivates the design of Algorithm 3.3: LDSD (Learnable Direction Sampling Descent).

Lines 3, 4, 7 of Algorithm 3.3 reflect the classical use of DGD estimator. In contrast, Lines 5 and 6 incorporate the proposed mechanism for learning the sampling direction. Specifically, to attain the values 𝔼[Ct|ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}\right|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}] of expected gradient alignment as large as possible, we adopt a reinforcement learning perspective by interpreting the mean vector μt\mu^{t} as a policy and 𝔼[Ct|ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}\right|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}] as the reward signal. Accordingly, at Line 3 of Algorithm 3.3, a direction vtv^{t} is sampled from the current policy, while at Lines 5 and 6 the policy is updated via a gradient ascent step.

Importantly, in practice the derivative of the expected gradient alignment ∇μ𝔼​[Ct|ℱt−1]|μ=μt\nabla_{\mu}\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}\right]\Big|_{\mu=\mu^{t}} is not accessible. Consequently, while the analysis employs the update in Line 5, for practical implementation we propose using a well-established policy gradient approach [Williams, 1992] from reinforcement learning. We refer to Sections 3.6 and 4 for further details on this implementation.

3.4 The dynamics of gradient alignment

Now we present Theorem 1, which characterizes the evolution of the expected gradient alignment 𝔼⁡[Ct|ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}\right] over a single iteration of Algorithm 3.3 and constitutes the core of the theoretical analysis of the proposed approach.

Theorem 1.

Let Assumption 1 hold and d≥16d\geq 16. Then for iterations of Algorithm 3.3 with ε≤𝒪⁡(d−32​cos⁡(βt)​(1−cos⁡(βt))​‖μt‖),γμt≤𝒪⁡(‖μt‖2),γxt≤𝒪⁡(cos2⁡(βt)​(1−cos⁡(βt))2L)\varepsilon\leq\mathcal{O}\left(d^{-\frac{3}{2}}\cos(\beta^{t})(1-\cos(\beta^{t}))\|\mu^{t}\|\right),\gamma_{\mu}^{t}\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\|\mu^{t}\|^{2}\right),\gamma_{x}^{t}\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\cos^{2}(\beta^{t})(1-\cos(\beta^{t}))^{2}}{L}\right) the following inequality holds:

𝔼[Ct+1|ℱt]=𝔼[Ct|ℱt−1]+γμt(cos⁡(βt)​(1−cos⁡(βt))24​‖μt‖)2,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t+1}\right|\mathcal{F}^{t}]=\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}\right|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}]+\gamma^{t}_{\mu}\left(\frac{\cos(\beta^{t})(1-\cos(\beta^{t}))}{24\|\mu^{t}\|}\right)^{2},

where βt\beta^{t} is the angle between μt\mu^{t} and ∇f​(xt)\nabla f(x^{t}).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 1, the values of 𝔼[Ct|ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}\right|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}] increase monotonically. This leads to acceleration in convergence guarantees in Lemma 1 and corresponds to an improvement of the policy μt\mu^{t}. At the same time, the theorem does not provide guarantees for a naive initialization μ0=0\mu^{0}=0 (Figure 1 illustrates that this point corresponds to a saddle point of the function 𝔼⁡[Ct|ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}\right]). It is consistent with the observation that ∇μ𝔼​[Ct|ℱt−1]|μ=0=0\nabla_{\mu}\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}\right]\Big|_{\mu=0}=0, together with the update rule in Line 6 of Algorithm 3.3, results in unchanged values of the policy: μt+1=μt\mu^{t+1}=\mu^{t} and, consequently, expected gradient alignment 𝔼⁡[Ct+1|ℱt]=𝔼⁡[Ct|ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t+1}|\mathcal{F}^{t}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}\right]. We also note that growth of the gradient alignment is not guaranteed in the cases of collinearity or orthogonality between μt\mu^{t} and ∇f​(xt)\nabla f(x^{t}), since the gradient of the alignment objective vanishes in these configurations. However, Algorithm 3.3 almost surely avoids these degenerate configurations when initialized at random, as they form a measure-zero set in the parameter space.

Intuition.

We now provide further intuition for the concepts underlying Theorem 1. Figure 1 depicts the landscape of the function 𝔼⁡[Ct∣ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}[C^{t}\mid\mathcal{F}^{t-1}] as a function of μt\mu^{t} in dimension d=2d=2.

The figure clearly reveals the intuitive saddle-like structure of the objective: increasing orthogonality of μt\mu^{t} and ∇f​(xt)\nabla f(x^{t}) leads to sampling vectors vtv^{t} that form large angles with ∇f​(xt)\nabla f(x^{t}) and therefore yield small values of CtC^{t}. In contrast, alignment between μt\mu^{t} and ∇f​(xt)\nabla f(x^{t}) results in larger values of both CtC^{t} and its conditional expectation. This landscape additionally exhibits symmetry with respect to the transformation μt↦−μt\mu^{t}\mapsto-\mu^{t}, reflecting the fact that CtC^{t} depends only on the squared cosine of the angle βt\beta^{t}.

Each iteration of Algorithm 3.3 performs a gradient ascent step on the function 𝔼⁡[Ct∣ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}[C^{t}\mid\mathcal{F}^{t-1}] with respect to μt\mu^{t}. From the RL perspective, it corresponds to a policy update driven by the observed reward signal 𝔼⁡[Ct∣ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}[C^{t}\mid\mathcal{F}^{t-1}]. Subsequently, a model parameter update is performed in Line 7, which in turn changes the direction of the true gradient ∇f​(xt)\nabla f(x^{t}). Geometrically, this corresponds to a rotation of the saddle while keeping μt\mu^{t} fixed. Assumption 1 on the Lipschitz continuity of ff, together with the explicit form of the update in Line 7, allows to bound the angle of this rotation in terms of the step size γxt\gamma_{x}^{t}. This bounded rotation may also be interpreted as a bounded change of the environment, which may reduce the relevance of the policy obtained at the previous iteration. The analysis in Theorem 1 is built upon carefully balancing these two competing effects: the gradient ascent step in μt\mu^{t} and the change in the direction of ∇f​(xt)\nabla f(x^{t}) induced by the update of the model parameters xtx^{t}.

The saddle structure of 𝔼⁡[Ct∣ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}[C^{t}\mid\mathcal{F}^{t-1}] immediately implies non-concavity. It prevents us from directly deriving its increase in Theorem 1 using standard results from gradient ascent theory, thereby significantly complicating the theoretical analysis. Due to the non-standard challenges and the resulting proof technique, we provide both a high-level sketch and a complete proof in Appendix B.

To characterize the full dynamics of 𝔼[Ct|ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}\right|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}] across the iterations of Algorithm 3.3 we prove the following result.

Lemma 2.

Let in the setting of Theorem 1 δ≤cos⁡(β0)≤1−δ\delta\leq\cos(\beta^{0})\leq 1-\delta with δ∈(0,12)\delta\in\left(0;\frac{1}{2}\right), ‖μt‖≤M\|\mu^{t}\|\leq M for all tt and ε=𝒪⁡(d−32​δ​M),γxt=𝒪⁡(δ2L)\varepsilon=\mathcal{O}\left(d^{-\frac{3}{2}}\delta M\right),\gamma_{x}^{t}=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\delta^{2}}{L}\right). Then 𝔼⁡[Ct|ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}\right] increase monotonically to the value

cos⁡(δ32​d+L​γxt+arccos⁡(1−δ))2​(1−e−1)=𝒪⁡(1)\cos\left(\frac{\delta}{32d}+L\gamma_{x}^{t}+\arccos(1-\delta)\right)^{2}(1-e^{-1})=\mathcal{O}(1)

and then never decrease below.

Lemma 2 establishes once the policy is initialized such that δ≤cos⁡(β0)≤1−δ\delta\leq\cos(\beta^{0})\leq 1-\delta, for an appropriate choice of γxt,γμt,ε\gamma_{x}^{t},\gamma_{\mu}^{t},\varepsilon the expected gradient alignment 𝔼[Ct|ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}\right|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}] increases monotonically up to a certain level and subsequently oscillates within a neighbourhood of 11. This stands in contrast to the 𝒪⁡(1/d)\mathcal{O}(1/d) behaviour established in Corollary 1.

3.5 Convergence Guaranties

Lemma 2 naturally leads to two complementary settings for policy initialization μ0\mu^{0}. The first corresponds to choosing μ0\mu^{0} randomly without any prior knowledge of the target function ff. This setup is analysed in Appendix B.1 and can be interpreted as a sequential growth of gradient alignment up to a saturation level. In particular, it leads to a non-standard convergence criterion formulated in terms of a weighted average of squared gradient norms evaluated along the iterates of the algorithm.

The second regime for μ0\mu^{0} initialization corresponds to leveraging prior information about the target function ff (the direction of the true gradient ∇f​(x0)\nabla f(x^{0}) at the initial point) to immediately operate in the phase of Lemma 2 where 𝔼[Ct|ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}\right|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}] oscillates in a neighbourhood of 11.

Lemma 3.

Let Assumptions 1, 2 be satisfied, d≥16d\geq 16 and μ0\mu^{0} collinear to ∇f​(x0)\nabla f(x^{0}). Then for iterations of Algorithm 3.3 with δ≤cos⁡(β0)≤1−δ\delta\leq\cos(\beta^{0})\leq 1-\delta, δ∈(0,12)\delta\in\left(0;\frac{1}{2}\right) and ε=𝒪⁡(d−32​δ​M),M=mint⁡{‖μt‖},γxt=𝒪⁡(δ2L),γμt=𝒪⁡(‖μt‖2)\varepsilon=\mathcal{O}\left(d^{-\frac{3}{2}}\delta M\right),M=\min_{t}\{\|\mu^{t}\|\},\gamma_{x}^{t}=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\delta^{2}}{L}\right),\gamma_{\mu}^{t}=\mathcal{O}\left(\|\mu^{t}\|^{2}\right), the following bound holds:

𝔼⁡[‖∇f​(x¯T)‖2]≤𝒪⁡(1T​γx)​(f⁡(x0)−f⁡(x∗)).\mathbb{E}[\|\nabla f(\overline{x}^{T})\|^{2}]\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{T\gamma_{x}}\right)(f(x^{0})-f(x^{*})).

Discussion.

We note that the dimension dd does not appear explicitly in the theoretical bounds of Lemma 3. In contrast, classical directional, coordinate or ZO methods incur the polynomial dependence on dd in their convergence guarantees [Nesterov and Spokoiny, 2017; Veprikov et al., 2024; Hanzely et al., 2018]. This slowdown is in fact unavoidable for uniformly random directions from the perspective of lower bounds [Lee and Sidford, 2013], which establish an inherent 𝒪⁡(d)\mathcal{O}(d) factor for standard ZO methods. Our approach overcomes this barrier by learning the parameters of the sampling distribution, effectively steering the sampled directions to better align with the gradient and thereby removing the explicit dependence on dd in the convergence rate.

It is worth noting that, in theory, the quality of the Monte-Carlo approximation gμtg_{\mu}^{t} obtained with a fixed number of samples vtv^{t} per iteration depends on the dimension dd. However, in practice a small number of samples, often 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1), is sufficient to obtain a stable Monte-Carlo estimate [Schulman et al., 2017].

Finally, we observe that after normalization the sampling distribution is invariant under simultaneous rescaling of the mean vector μ\mu and the variance ε2\varepsilon^{2}. This invariance also appears in choice of ε∼d−32​δ​M≤d−32​δ​‖μt‖\varepsilon\sim d^{-\frac{3}{2}}\delta M\leq d^{-\frac{3}{2}}\delta\|\mu^{t}\| in the analysis. This suggests that constraining ‖μ‖=1\|\mu\|=1 may be a natural design choice and a direction for future work.

3.6 Toy Experiment

To validate the theoretical results, we conduct a toy experiment consisting of training a linear regression model on the a9a [Chang and Lin, 2011] dataset with access to directional derivatives. As a baseline, we consider an algorithm that employs the estimator with KK Monte Carlo samples:

gxt=1K​∑k=1Kv¯kt​⟨v¯kt,∇f​(xt)⟩,\displaystyle g_{x}^{t}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\overline{v}_{k}^{t}\langle\overline{v}_{k}^{t},\nabla f(x^{t})\rangle, (5)

with vkt∼𝒩⁡(0,I)v_{k}^{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). For LDSD, we use the same approximation (5) with the choice vkt∼𝒩⁡(μt,ε2​I)v_{k}^{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu^{t},\varepsilon^{2}I). For proposed learning mechanism we apply a log-derivative trick [Williams, 1992] to derive a Monte Carlo estimator of ∇μ𝔼​[Ct|ℱt−1]|μ=μt\nabla_{\mu}\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}\right]\Big|_{\mu=\mu^{t}} from the Line 5 of Algorithm 3.3. We denote the density of a Gaussian distribution by πμ​(⋅)\pi_{\mu}(\cdot) and introduce Ckt=⟨vkt¯,∇f​(xt)¯⟩2C_{k}^{t}=\langle{\overline{v_{k}^{t}},\overline{\nabla f(x^{t})}}\rangle^{2} for each sampled direction vktv^{t}_{k}. Accordingly,

∇μ𝔼​[Ct|ℱt−1]|μ=μt\displaystyle\nabla_{\mu}\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}\right]\Big|_{\mu=\mu^{t}} =∫Ct​(∇μ​log​πμt)​d​πμt≈1K​∑k=1KCkt​(∇μ​log​πμt​(vkt)).\displaystyle=\int C^{t}\left(\nabla_{\mu}\log\pi_{\mu^{t}}\right)\mathrm{d}\pi_{\mu^{t}}\approx\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}C_{k}^{t}\left(\nabla_{\mu}\log\pi_{\mu^{t}}(v_{k}^{t})\right).

Since πμt​(⋅)\pi_{\mu^{t}}(\cdot) is a Gaussian distribution density, we have ∇μ​log​πμt​(vkt)=vkt−μtε2\nabla_{\mu}\log\pi_{\mu^{t}}(v_{k}^{t})=\frac{v_{k}^{t}-\mu^{t}}{\varepsilon^{2}}. For policy updates we utilize

gμt=1K​∑k=1K(Ckt−bt)​vkt−μtε2,\displaystyle g_{\mu}^{t}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left(C^{t}_{k}-b^{t}\right)\frac{v_{k}^{t}-\mu^{t}}{\varepsilon^{2}},

where bt=1K​∑k=1KCktb^{t}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}C^{t}_{k} is a mean-baseline, introduced to reduce the estimator variance [Williams, 1992].

We set K=5K=5 both for the baseline and LDSD and compare them in terms of the alignment between the true gradient and its estimator cos⁡(gxt,∇f​(xt))\cos(g_{x}^{t},\nabla f(x^{t})), as well as the norm of the gradient ‖∇f​(xt)‖\|\nabla f(x^{t})\|: the quantity involved in convergence guaranties. The results are reported in Figure 2.

The first plot in Figure 2 reveals learning the sampling direction in LDSD indeed leads to strong alignment between the estimator gμtg_{\mu}^{t} and the true gradient ∇f​(xt)\nabla f(x^{t}). This behaviour fully agrees with Lemma 2 and the intuition discussed in Section 3: the alignment initially increases monotonically and subsequently oscillates in a neighbourhood of 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1).

4  Zero-order Framework

Building on Algorithm 3.3, which presented the first-order instantiation of our update rules, we now develop the corresponding ZO formulation in Algorithm 4 by replacing the directional derivative gxtg_{x}^{t} with a zero-order oracle (2), and the gradient gμtg_{\mu}^{t} with its REINForCE estimation [Williams, 1992]. Both substitutions yield unbiased estimators of the corresponding first-order gradients [Feng and Wang, 2023], thereby preserving the theoretical structure of the original algorithm in a purely zero-order setting.

The selection of v∗tv_{*}^{t} in Line 4 of Algorithm 4 implements a lightweight, direction-wise greedy search among the KK sampled candidates: by choosing the perturbation that empirically yields the smallest objective after a forward evaluation, the method biases the subsequent xx-update (Line 7 of Algorithm 4) toward directions that have demonstrated the strongest instantaneous decrease in ff. This selection improves the practical utility of a limited number of oracle queries and typically reduces the variance of the chosen search direction, at the cost of introducing an intentional selection bias in the sampled direction for the xx-update.

Aside from those mechanics and the replacement of true gradients by zero-order estimates, Algorithm 4 preserves the structural update logic of Algorithm 3.3. The procedure preserves the forward-only nature of ZO methods, requires K+1K+1 forward evaluations per iteration, and concentrates sampling mass on empirically useful directions through online updates of μt\mu^{t}. While classical ZO schemes typically use K=1K=1, we set K=5K=5 in our experiments as an empirically chosen compromise between selection quality and oracle cost. An ablation over KK is provided in Section 5.3.

It is important to note that this framework is not a standalone optimizer but a plug-in module: any existing ZO estimator for the parameter update can be combined with the adaptive sampling routine to improve empirical convergence. In particular, the update at line 7 of Algorithm 4 is modular and may be replaced by the parameter-update rule of any other ZO optimizer. This enables straightforward integration of the adaptive sampling mechanism, while leaving the base optimizer’s update logic intact.

5  Experiments

In this section, we present an empirical evaluation of the proposed zero-order optimization framework for large language model fine-tuning.

5.1 Experimental setup

Fine-Tuning Task and Schemes. We evaluate the proposed zero-order methods on the SST-2 sentiment classification benchmark [Socher et al., 2013], following the experimental protocol of [Zhang et al., 2024]. SST-2 is a standard supervised benchmark for sentence-level binary sentiment classification and is commonly used to assess fine-tuning procedures for language models.

Models. Experiments are performed on two representative models: RoBERTa-Large [Liu et al., 2019] and OPT-1.3B [Zhang et al., 2022]. These models span different architectures and parameter counts, allowing us to examine the behavior of ZO algorithms across realistic fine-tuning settings while keeping the experimental scope focused.

Baselines. We use our framework on established zero-order baselines reported in [Zhang et al., 2024]: ZO-SGD [Ghadimi and Lan, 2013], ZO-AdaMM [Chen et al., 2019], JAGUAR SignSGD [Petrov et al., 2025]. All experiments follow the evaluation of [Zhang et al., 2024] to ensure a fair comparison. Training details are deferred to Appendix A.2.

Comparison procedure. For a fair and controlled evaluation we compare each baseline in two variants: (i) the original baseline implementation, and (ii) the same baseline augmented with our zero-order adaptive sampling framework (Algorithm 4). Crucially, in (ii) we do not change any of the original optimizer hyperparameters from (i) (e.g., learning rate, momentum), those remain exactly as in the base method. The only hyperparameters we tune are those introduced by our framework.

Since Algorithm 4 performs 66 ZO oracle calls (forward passes) when K=5K=5, we compare baseline methods under a fixed budget of oracle calls rather than a fixed number of iterations to ensure fair evaluation. This leads to two natural comparison strategies for the baselines: either perform 66 oracle calls per iteration (using K=5K=5 samples), or perform more iterations with 22 oracle calls per iteration (using K=1K=1). Both variants are presented in Table 1. This design ensures that performance differences arise from the adaptive sampling module itself rather than from differences in computational budget.

5.2 Results

Table 1 reports SST2 test accuracy for OPT-1.3B and RoBERTa-Large under different fine-tuning schemes.

Discussion. The results show that replacing Gaussian sampling with our adaptive direction sampling produces consistent improvements across models, optimizers, and fine-tuning modalities. Notably, merely increasing the number of probes with Gaussian sampling does not yield the same benefit: performance gains arise from the combination of multiple candidates and adaptive selection. These findings indicate that our sampling scheme yields more informative finite-difference probes and reduces variance in the resulting ZO gradient proxies. Because the framework is plug-and-play, it improves practical convergence of existing ZO methods without altering their core update rules.

5.3 Ablation Studies

In this section, we provide several ablation studies on hyperparameters from Algorithm 4. In all experiments we use SST-2 dataset with the RoBERTa-large model. Figure 3(a) shows accuracy rising with KK up to K=5K=5 and then slightly falling; (b) exhibits improvement as γμ\gamma_{\mu} increases until an intermediate optimum after which performance degrades; and (c) displays a U-shaped dependence on ε\varepsilon with a clear peak where our method outperforms the Gaussian baseline. These results motivate the default hyperparameter choices used in our experiments.

6  Conclusion

In this work, we introduce a novel zero-order optimization framework that treats the sampling distribution over perturbation directions as a learnable policy. Theoretically, we provide convergence guarantees with no explicit dependence on dimension dd, in stark contrast to the 𝒪⁡(d)\mathcal{O}(d) degradation inherent in classical zero-order methods. This represents a significant advancement for ZO optimization, achieved by adaptively learning the mean of the sampling distribution to maintain high gradient alignment throughout training.

Empirically, we validate our framework on LLM fine-tuning benchmarks, demonstrating consistent improvements over established ZO baselines including ZO-SGD, ZO-AdaMM, and JAGUAR SignSGD. Our framework operates as a plug-and-play module that enhances existing ZO optimizers without modifying their core hyperparameters. Extensive ablation studies confirm the robustness and practical applicability of our approach.

Due to the non-standard challenges and the resulting proof technique, we provide high-level sketch before the proof.

Proof Sketch of Theorem 1.

The proof of Theorem 1 is deferred to Section B. It tracks the joint evolution of two quantities: the gradient ∇f​(xt)\nabla f(x^{t}) and the mean vector μt\mu^{t}. The main steps are as follows:

(i) We first reduce the gradient dynamics using Assumption 1, which yields a relation of the form

We note that 𝔼[Ct|ℱt−1]=F∇f​(xt)¯(μt)\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}\right|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}]=F_{\overline{\nabla f(x^{t})}}(\mu^{t}). Then, we need to reduce μt+1\mu^{t+1} to μt\mu^{t} in the RHS of (9) to obtain a recursion on expected gradient alignment.

(ii) The core objective is to prove strict monotonic growth of expected gradient alignment 𝔼[Ct+1|ℱt]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t+1}\right|\mathcal{F}^{t}]. Achieving this requires carefully isolating a positive contribution that dominates the drift ata^{t} induced by changes in ∇f​(xt)\nabla f(x^{t}). Then, to enable a quantitative analysis, we establish smoothness of the function Fz​(μ)F_{z}(\mu) with respect to μt\mu^{t} via a uniform bound on the Hessian norm. This yields an inequality of the form

F∇f​(xt)¯​(μt+1)≥F∇f​(xt)¯​(μt)+(γμt−L~​γμt22)​‖∇F∇f​(xt)¯​(μt)‖2.\displaystyle F_{\overline{\nabla f(x^{t})}}(\mu^{t+1})\geq F_{\overline{\nabla f(x^{t})}}(\mu^{t})+\left(\gamma^{t}_{\mu}-\frac{\tilde{L}{\gamma^{t}_{\mu}}^{2}}{2}\right)\|\nabla F_{\overline{\nabla f(x^{t})}}(\mu^{t})\|^{2}. (10)

(iii) Combining the above relations (9) and (10) yields a recursive inequality for 𝔼[Ct+1|ℱt]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t+1}\right|\mathcal{F}^{t}]. To ensure a positive increment, it suffices to lower bound the contribution of the last term in (10). To this end, we decompose the expectation over uu in Fz​(μ)F_{z}(\mu) definition into integrals over an inner region u≤‖μt‖2​εu\leq\frac{\|\mu^{t}\|}{2\varepsilon} and its complement.

The integral over the outer region is controlled by choosing ε≲‖μ‖​d−12\varepsilon\lesssim\|\mu\|d^{-\frac{1}{2}}, allowing us to apply Gaussian concentration inequalities for Lipschitz functions [Boucheron et al., 2013].

The inner-region contribution is analysed via a Taylor expansion with a Lagrange remainder. Each term is treated separately. First, symmetry considerations eliminate zero order term. Second, the second-order term is controlled using the previously established Hessian bound. Third, the Laurent-Massart inequalities [Laurent and Massart, 2000] serve as a core ingredient for extracting the required positive increment from the first order term.

Putting these estimates together with (9), (10) and balancing the competing effects yields the final bound.

B.1 Initialization with no prior information

Lemma 2 naturally leads to two complementary settings. The first is formalized in Lemma 5 and corresponds to initializing the policy without any prior knowledge of the target function ff.

Lemma 5.

Let Assumptions 1, 2 be satisfied and d≥16d\geq 16. Then for iterations of Algorithm 3.3 with δ≤cos⁡(β0)≤1−δ\delta\leq\cos(\beta^{0})\leq 1-\delta, δ∈(0,12)\delta\in\left(0;\frac{1}{2}\right) and ε=d−32​δ​M960,γxt=δ23⋅214⋅52​L,γμt=‖μt‖2640\varepsilon=\frac{d^{-\frac{3}{2}}\delta M}{960},\gamma_{x}^{t}=\frac{\delta^{2}}{3\cdot 2^{14}\cdot 5^{2}L},\gamma_{\mu}^{t}=\frac{\|\mu^{t}\|^{2}}{640} the following bound holds:

∑t=0T−11T​𝔼​[Bt​‖∇f​(xt)‖2]≤2​f⁡(x0)−f⁡(x∗)T​γxt,\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\frac{1}{T}\mathbb{E}\left[B^{t}\|\nabla f(x^{t})\|^{2}\right]\leq 2\frac{f(x^{0})-f(x^{*})}{T\gamma_{x}^{t}}, (54)

where M=mint⁡{‖μt‖}M=\min_{t}\{\|\mu^{t}\|\} and Bt=min⁡{𝔼⁡[C0]+t⋅δ23⋅212⋅52;cos⁡(δ32​d+L​γxt+arccos⁡(1−δ))2​(1−e−1)}B^{t}=\min\left\{\mathbb{E}[C^{0}]+t\cdot\frac{\delta^{2}}{3\cdot 2^{12}\cdot 5^{2}};\cos\left(\frac{\delta}{32d}+L\gamma_{x}^{t}+\arccos(1-\delta)\right)^{2}(1-e^{-1})\right\}.

Proof.

We start from the result of Lemma 1. The choice of γxt=δ23⋅214⋅52​L\gamma_{x}^{t}=\frac{\delta^{2}}{3\cdot 2^{14}\cdot 5^{2}L} guarantees

γxt−L​γxt22≥γxt2.\displaystyle\gamma_{x}^{t}-\frac{L{\gamma_{x}^{t}}^{2}}{2}\geq\frac{\gamma_{x}^{t}}{2}. (55)

Subsequently, Theorem 1 and Lemma 2 justifies

𝔼⁡[Ct|ℱt−1]≥Bt.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}\right]\geq B^{t}. (56)

Substitution (55), (56) into Lemma 1 and rearranging the terms finish the proof. ∎

Notably, in this setting, substituting 𝔼[Ct|ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}\right|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}] behaviour described in Lemma 2 yields a non-standard convergence criterion, namely convergence in terms of a weighted average of squared gradient norms. The weights increase with the iteration index until reaching a saturation level. Such a result may be more transparent for practical scenarios such as memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning, where the algorithm outputs the final iterate rather than an averaged solution.

We also note that Lemma 5 relies on a uniform-in-iteration lower bound of the form cos⁡(βt)>δ\cos(\beta^{t})>\delta, which results in a fixed step size γxt\gamma_{x}^{t} and a constant additive increase of 𝔼[Ct|ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}\right|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}] per iteration. However, as the policy improves, cos⁡(βt)\cos(\beta^{t}) increases, which simultaneously accelerates the growth of 𝔼[Ct|ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}\right|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}] and allows for larger admissible step sizes γxt\gamma_{x}^{t}. Consequently, the uniform bound becomes loose after a certain number of iterations and does not fully capture these acceleration effects in the theoretical rate. Along similar lines, bounds of the type used in the proof of Lemma 1 yield average values on the order of 1d\frac{1}{d} both for δ2\delta^{2} (consequently for γxt\gamma_{x}^{t}) and 𝔼⁡[C0]\mathbb{E}[C^{0}]. It introduces a factor d2d^{2} in the rate of Lemma 5 during the initial phase and results in growth of 𝔼[Ct|ℱt−1]\mathbb{E}\left[C^{t}\right|\mathcal{F}^{t-1}] on the order of 1d\frac{1}{d} per iteration.
